d.t: (transitive) To continue in (a course or mode of action); to not intermit or fall from; to uphold or maintain.
d.e: to keep silence;  to keep possession

d.t: (transitive) To remain faithful to a given promise or word.
d.e: to keep one's word;  to keep one's promise

d.t: (transitive) To hold the status of something.
(intransitive) To hold or be held in a state.
(obsolete) To wait for, keep watch for.
(intransitive, cricket) To act as wicket-keeper.
d.e: Godfrey Evans kept for England for many years.

d.t: (intransitive, obsolete) To take care; to be solicitous; to watch.
(intransitive, obsolete) To be in session; to take place.
d.e: School keeps today.

d.t: (transitive) To observe; to adhere to; to fulfill; to not swerve from or violate.
(transitive, dated, by extension) To visit (a place) often; to frequent.
(transitive, dated) To observe or celebrate (a holiday).
d.e: to keep the Sabbath

d.t: (transitive, Singapore, Wales) To put (something) back (to its original location or appropriate place); to put away.
d.e: Please keep these books.

d.t: (historical) The main tower of a castle or fortress, located within the castle walls.
The food or money required to keep someone alive and healthy; one's support, maintenance.
d.e: He works as a cobbler's apprentice for his keep.

d.t: The state of being kept; hence, the resulting condition; case.
d.e: to be in good keep

d.t: (engineering) A cap for holding something, such as a journal box, in place.
(obsolete) The act or office of keeping; custody; guard; care; heed; charge; notice.
(obsolete) That which is kept in charge; a charge.
(euphemistic, obsolete) A mistress (the other woman in an extramarital relationship, generally including sexual relations).
(transitive) To maintain; to preserve; to prevent from deteriorating or falling.
(transitive, idiomatic) To continue with (work, etc).
d.e: Keep up the good work, team!

d.t: (intransitive, idiomatic) To maintain position; to prevent oneself from falling behind; to stay even or ahead of another while walking, driving, etc.
d.e: They ran so fast I could hardly keep up.

d.t: To ensure that one remains well-informed about something.
d.e: I always try to keep up with (or "keep up on") current affairs.

d.t: To prevent someone from going to bed or to sleep
d.e: The crying baby kept me up all night

d.t: (obsolete, printing) To use capital letters as much as reasonable.
(countable) An object designed to open and close a lock or to activate or deactivate something, especially a length of metal inserted into a narrow opening on the lock to which it is matched (keyed).
d.e: This key is to the backdoor.

d.t: An object designed to fit between two other objects (such as a shaft and a wheel) in a mechanism and maintain their relative orientation.
(figurative) A crucial step or requirement.
d.e: Persistence is the key to solving this problem.

d.t: Senses relating to a guide that identifies information.
Senses relating to a set of features that modify the output of a device.
(music) A scale or group of pitches constituting the basis of a musical composition.
d.e: the key of B-flat major

d.t: Senses of items with visual similarity to a key or group of keys on a keyring.
Senses related to colors.
(historical) A manual electrical switching device primarily used for the transmission of Morse code.
The degree of roughness, or the ability of a surface to retain an applied liquid, such as paint or glue.
d.e: The door panel should be sanded down carefully to provide a good key for the new paint.

d.t: One of a string of small islands.
d.e: the Florida Keys

d.t: (slang) A kilogram, especially of a recreational drug.
Alternative form of quay.
(Australian rules football) A key position player (a tall forward or defender).
Indispensable, supremely important.
d.e: He is the key player on his soccer team.

d.t: Important, salient.
d.e: She makes several key points.

d.t: To fit (a lock) with a key.
To fit (pieces of a mechanical assembly) with a key to maintain the orientation between them.
To mark or indicate with a symbol indicating membership in a class.
d.e:
2007, Stephen Blake Mettee, Michelle Doland, and Doris Hall, compilers, The American Directory of Writer's Guidelines, 6th ("2007–2008") edition, →ISBN, page 757,
Indicate the comparative value of each heading by keying it with a number in pencil, in the left margin, as follows: […]

d.t: (telegraphy and radio telegraphy) To depress (a telegraph key).
(radio) To operate (the transmitter switch of a two-way radio).
(computing) (more usually to key in) To enter (information) by typing on a keyboard or keypad.
d.e: Our instructor told us to key in our user IDs.

d.t: (colloquial) To vandalize (a car, etc.) by scratching with an implement such as a key.
d.e: He keyed the car that had taken his parking spot.

d.t: To link (as one might do with a key or legend).
(intransitive, biology, chiefly taxonomy) To be identified as a certain taxon when using a key.
(advertising, transitive) To modify (an advertisement) so as to target a particular group or demographic.
To attune to; to set at; to pitch.
To fasten or secure firmly; to fasten or tighten with keys or wedges.
A type, race or category; a group of entities that have common characteristics such that they may be grouped together.
d.e: What kind of (a) person are you?

d.t: A makeshift or otherwise atypical specimen.
d.e: The opening served as a kind of window.

d.t: (archaic) One's inherent nature; character, natural disposition.
(archaic) Family, lineage.
d.e:
My young love said to me, My mother won’t mind
And my father won’t slight you for your lack of kind.

d.t: (archaic) Manner.
Goods or services used as payment, as e.g. in barter.
d.e: in kind

d.t: Equivalent means used as response to an action.
d.e: in kind

d.t: (Christianity) Each of the two elements of the communion service, bread and wine.
(type theory) The type of a type constructor or a higher-order type operator.
d.e: The kind of any primitive data type is *, corresponding to a nullary constructor.

d.t: (Caribbean, in compounds) Food in a particular category.
Having a benevolent, courteous, friendly, generous, gentle, liberal, sympathetic, or warm-hearted nature or disposition, marked by consideration for – and service to – others.
Affectionate.
d.e: a kind man; a kind heart

d.t: Favorable.
Mild, gentle, forgiving
d.e: The years have been kind to Richard Gere; he ages well.

d.t: Gentle; tractable; easily governed.
d.e: a horse kind in harness

d.t: (obsolete) Characteristic of the species; belonging to one's nature; natural; native.
(transitive) To perceive the truth or factuality of; to be certain of; to be certain that.
d.e: I know that I’m right and you’re wrong.

d.t: (intransitive) To be or become aware or cognizant.
d.e: Did you know Michelle and Jack were getting divorced? ― Yes, I knew.

d.t: (transitive) To be aware of; to be cognizant of.
d.e: Did you know Michelle and Jack were getting divorced? ― Yes, I knew.

d.t: (intransitive, obsolete) To be acquainted (with another person).
(transitive) To be acquainted or familiar with; to have encountered.
d.e: I know your mother, but I've never met your father.

d.t: (transitive) To experience.
d.e: Their relationship knew ups and downs.

d.t: To understand or have a grasp of through experience or study.
d.e: Let me do it. I know how it works.

d.t: (transitive) To be able to distinguish, to discern, particularly by contrast or comparison; to recognize the nature of.
d.e: to know a person's face or figure

d.t: (transitive) To recognize as the same (as someone or something previously encountered) after an absence or change.
(intransitive) To have knowledge; to have information, be informed.
d.e: It is vital that he not know.

d.t: (transitive) To be able to play or perform (a song or other piece of music).
d.e: Do you know "Blueberry Hill"?

d.t: (transitive) To have indexed and have information about within one's database.
(rare) Knowledge; the state of knowing.
Knowledge; the state of knowing. (Now confined to the fixed phrase in the know.)
Alternative form of knowe (“hill, knoll”).
(Singlish) Used at the end of a sentence to draw attention to information one thinks the listener should keep in mind.
d.e: Make sure you water the plants, know…

d.t: (Singlish) Synonym of you know (used as a conversational discourse marker, to emphasize something)
The fact of knowing about something; general understanding or familiarity with a subject, place, situation etc.
d.e: His knowledge of Iceland was limited to what he'd seen on the Travel Channel.

d.t: Awareness of a particular fact or situation; a state of having been informed or made aware of something.
Intellectual understanding; the state of appreciating truth or information.
d.e: Knowledge consists in recognizing the difference between good and bad decisions.

d.t: Familiarity or understanding of a particular skill, branch of learning etc.
d.e: Does your friend have any knowledge of hieroglyphs, perchance?

d.t: (philosophical) Justified true belief
(archaic or law) Sexual intimacy or intercourse (now usually in phrase carnal knowledge).
(obsolete) Information or intelligence about something; notice.
The total of what is known; all information and products of learning.
d.e: His library contained the accumulated knowledge of the Greeks and Romans.

d.t: (countable) Something that can be known; a branch of learning; a piece of information; a science.
(obsolete) Acknowledgement.
(obsolete) Notice, awareness.
(UK, informal) The deep familiarity with certain routes and places of interest required by taxicab drivers working in London, England.
(obsolete) To confess as true; to acknowledge.
